The post-hoc re-ranking component cannot be positioned as a distinct contribution.

input.statement: Final positioning verdict: a post-hoc temporal re-ranking component cannot be positioned as a distinct contribution. Temporal scoring with decay is implemented (learnable decay inside graph retrieval), validity-aware filtering is prescribed and partially implemented (ontology-driven pre-retrieval filtering by temporal validity), the legal-retrieval review states the bitemporal/point-in-time requirement and even its detection criterion ('can the system return the text that was in force at T') but reports no benchmarked empirical comparison, and a leading legal benchmark documents that retrieval-oriented legal benchmarks do not assess whether retrieved provisions remain in force. The defensible remaining delta is therefore the implemented measurement: version-level point-in-time recovery and contamination on near-duplicate amended clauses with recency-decoupled strata, plus the comparative result on whether the published recency-decay hybrid suffices. Note that even the metric is conceptually prescribed by prior work, so novelty is implementation and evidence rather than formulation.

input.confidence_basis: Convergent comparison evidence across five sources: the closest framework reports no empirical comparison, decay-based temporal scoring is implemented elsewhere, validity-aware legal filtering is prescribed and partially implemented, and a leading legal benchmark states that in-force status of retrieved provisions is not assessed. Residual uncertainty concerns publication value rather than factual overlap.
input.resolution: Resolved: the post-hoc temporal re-ranking component cannot be positioned as a distinct contribution. Decay-based temporal scoring is already implemented (learnable exponential decay inside graph-based retrieval), validity-aware retrieval is already prescribed and partially implemented as an ontology-driven pre-retrieval filter, and the requirement and even its detection criterion are articulated in the legal-retrieval literature - which nonetheless reports no benchmarked empirical comparison of existing systems. The defensible delta is the implemented measurement: version-level point-in-time recovery and contamination on near-duplicate amended clauses with recency-decoupled strata, plus the comparative finding about whether the published recency-decay hybrid suffices. Caveat to state honestly in any write-up: the metric is conceptually prescribed by prior work, so the contribution is evidence and implementation, not formulation.

input.direction: Replace the original mechanism-efficacy question with a measurement question. The study now asks what version-level point-in-time retrieval failure rates existing retrievers exhibit on clause-versioned amended legal text, and whether a valid-time gate reduces version contamination where the published recency-decay hybrid does not. Drop the temporal relevance component, the retrieval-agnostic framing and the temporal benchmark as contribution claims; keep them as adopted components and as a reusable artifact. State in the write-up that the metric is conceptually prescribed by prior work and that the contribution is the implemented benchmark, the per-retriever evidence and the possible negative result that decay suffices.
input.hypothesis: Existing retrievers, including the published recency-decay hybrid, exhibit measurable version-level point-in-time failures on amended legal text whose successive clause versions are near-duplicates, and the failure rate is highest on queries whose in-force version is not the latest; valid-time gating reduces those failures where decay does not.
input.rationale: Every comparison in this phase converges: the mechanism is implemented elsewhere in decay form, validity-aware filtering is prescribed and partially implemented, the legal-retrieval review states the required test criterion yet reports no empirical comparison, and a leading legal benchmark documents that in-force status of retrieved provisions is not assessed. The only claim not contradicted by this evidence is a measured one, so the research question must change from whether the component helps to what the failure rates are and whether decay suffices. This deserves investigation next because it is the smallest claim the evidence supports, it is falsifiable in both directions, and the negative branch is itself a contribution about where temporal handling belongs in legal RAG.
input.research_question: What version-level point-in-time retrieval failure rates (selection of superseded or not-yet-in-force clause versions) do sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers - including the published lexical+dense+recency-decay hybrid - exhibit on continuously amended legal text with near-duplicate successive clause versions, and does valid-time (as-of) gating reduce those failures where recency decay does not?

input.description: The entire direction assumes existing retrievers actually fail at version selection on amended legal text. If semantic or hybrid retrieval already places the in-force clause first most of the time - for instance because amendments change enough wording, or because the current consolidated text dominates the corpus - then the measured failure rate is near zero, the problem premise fails, and there is no gap for a temporal gate to close. No retrieved work reports a version-level failure rate for any retriever, so the magnitude is entirely unknown.
input.question: Do existing retrievers already select the correct in-force clause version most of the time on amended legal text, leaving no measurable version-confusion problem?
input.rationale: The premise of the study is that version confusion is common, but no retrieved work measures it; the experiment's first descriptive result decides whether the rest of the programme is worth running.
